sections.h2: What should a Dearborn homeowner know before selling?
sections.html:
Dearborn sellers face one step that most Michigan sellers never see: the city requires a Certificate of Occupancy before a house can close. It comes from a city inspection, and it is issued in the buyer's name, so the timing has to be planned from the day you decide to sell.

Dearborn is an inner-ring suburb in Wayne County that borders Detroit on the north and east, about seven miles west of downtown Detroit. The city covers roughly 24.5 square miles and grew up on both banks of the Rouge River. The neighboring village of Fordson, once called Springwells, merged with Dearborn in a 1928 vote.

The Ford Motor Company world headquarters, the Ford River Rouge complex and The Henry Ford museum campus shape the local housing market. Many owners here live close to a Ford job, a hospital or one of the two colleges, and buyers often start their search with commute time.

sections.h2: How does the Dearborn pre-sale inspection work?
sections.html:
The seller, the listing agent or a legally appointed power of attorney files a residential inspection request with the city's Economic Development Department and pays the fee with it. City staff then call to set the visit, which takes about 45 minutes. An adult aged 18 or older must be home for the whole inspection.

The inspector checks basic safety and property maintenance against the city's minimum housing standards, then issues a written report. Every item on that report counts as a code violation and has to be fixed and re-inspected. The sequence runs like this:

  • Submit the application and payment.
  • Wait for staff to schedule the inspection.
  • Be present for the walk-through and keep the report.
  • Correct each listed item within one year of the first inspection date.
  • Request a re-inspection and pass it.
  • Email the buyer's name to the city sales address and say whether the buyer will live in the house, so the certificate can be prepared.

An inspection report stays valid for one year, so a house that falls out of contract can be relisted without starting over, provided the year has not run out.

sections.h2: Which schools, employers and roads matter to Dearborn buyers?
sections.html:
Dearborn Public Schools operates 34 schools and serves more than 18,000 students, making it the fourth-largest district in Michigan. The main high schools are Fordson High School, Dearborn High School and Edsel Ford High School. Private and charter options include Divine Child, Henry Ford Academy inside Greenfield Village, and Advanced Technology Academy.

The University of Michigan-Dearborn and Henry Ford College sit next to each other on Evergreen Road. Ford is the largest employer by a wide margin in the city's 2022 financial report, followed by Beaumont Health and the school district. Carhartt, AAA Michigan and Cleveland-Cliffs Dearborn Works also appear among the top ten.

Buyers who commute tend to ask about travel time, and the Census lists a mean of 21.7 minutes for Dearborn workers. Fairlane Town Center, the Henry Ford Centennial Library and the Fair Lane estate give the city's middle section a lot of green and civic space, much of it kept open on land Henry Ford once assembled.

sections.h2: How do Dearborn property taxes work for a seller?
sections.html:
The city bills property tax twice a year, and the summer and winter bills cover different taxing bodies. Knowing which bill is open at closing tells you how much to expect on the settlement statement.

  • Summer taxes are levied July 1 and due September 14. They include school tax, city tax and the county-allocated operating tax. Owners can split them into installments due September 14, November 14 and January 14 for a one-time $3 fee.
  • Winter taxes are levied December 1 and due February 14, with no installment option. They carry the rest of the county tax and the city's combined sewer overflow debt.
  • Ask the Treasury Division for a payoff figure in writing before closing, so the title company pays the right bill.

Treasury is at the Dearborn Administrative Center, 16901 Michigan Avenue, open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The Assessment Department is in the same building and can be reached at 313-943-2140 for questions about assessed or taxable value.

sections.h2: What costs and filings come with a Dearborn sale?
sections.html:
State law puts the real estate transfer tax on the seller. The state rate is $3.75 for each $500 of value under MCL 207.525, and the county adds 55 cents per $500 in a county under 2,000,000 residents under MCL 207.504. Ask the Wayne County Register of Deeds to confirm the current county figure before you set a net sheet.

Several transfers are exempt from the state tax, including a conveyance from a parent to a child or from a grandparent to a grandchild, a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and a land contract where title has not yet passed (MCL 207.526). A deed that states a sale price of less than $100 is also exempt.

Two filings follow the sale. The buyer must tell the assessor about the transfer within 45 days under MCL 211.27a, and the assessed value for the next year resets to the state equalized value, which the city's assessment guide calls uncapping. If you claimed the principal residence exemption, ask the Dearborn assessor for the form that removes your name from it.

sections.h2: Which selling route fits a Dearborn house with open inspection items?
sections.html:
A listed sale keeps your price high but requires you to finish every cited repair before closing. A sale to an investor who plans to rent the house or renovate it still needs the certificate, and the city asks whether the buyer will occupy the home. A direct sale lets you agree on who pays for repairs, which is useful when the inspection list is long and the one-year window is short.

A long list is the usual reason a Dearborn sale slips. Get the inspection scheduled early, ask the buyer in writing who handles the corrections, and keep the report with your closing file.

faqs.q: Do I need a Certificate of Occupancy to sell my Dearborn house?
faqs.a: Yes. The city requires one before closing, and it follows a pre-sale inspection. You, your agent or a power of attorney requests the inspection, fixes any violations, passes a re-inspection and then emails the buyer's name to city staff so the certificate can be issued in that name.

faqs.q: How long is a Dearborn inspection report valid?
faqs.a: One year from the date of the first inspection. You have that same year to correct every listed violation and pass the re-inspection, so a sale that falls through does not force a second full inspection if you relist inside the year.

faqs.q: When are Dearborn property taxes due?
faqs.a: Summer taxes are due September 14 and winter taxes are due February 14. Summer taxes can be paid in three installments on September 14, November 14 and January 14, while winter taxes must be paid in full.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax on a Dearborn sale?
faqs.a: The seller. State law makes the grantor liable for the tax, which is $3.75 per $500 of value at the state level plus the county rate. Some transfers are exempt, such as deeds from a parent to a child.

faqs.q: What happens to my taxable value after I sell?
faqs.a: It resets for the buyer. In the year after a transfer of ownership the taxable value equals the state equalized value, and the inflation cap applies again from the following year. Your own exemption stops once you rescind it with the assessor.
